A checklist before you move funds between accounts

A mutual fund or ETF is not tax-exempt by itself. Inside a TFSA, CRA says income such as interest, dividends or capital gains is generally tax-free, even when you withdraw. The same fund held in a non-registered account is taxed under the ordinary rules: CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains that interest, dividends and capital gains distributed by a fund are reported in the year they are paid, even when the distribution is reinvested in more units.

A positive value means that placement leaves more after-tax money than putting the bond fund in the TFSA first. Annual tax on interest favours sheltering bonds; tax-free compounding of a higher expected equity return favours sheltering equity. The crossover depends entirely on the entered returns and tax rates.

A practical note: removing a fixed set of months gives the same ending value whatever order the months occur in. Order matters only once a person must choose an exit date, and that is where clustering becomes decisive.

A single balanced fund held in both accounts, the “same mix” bar, gives up a little potential optimization in exchange for simplicity and an identical risk profile in each account. For many households that trade-off is reasonable. Provincial tax, foreign withholding tax on foreign dividends, dividend gross-up and credit details, and personal circumstances can all change the result; a tax professional can review the specifics.

Room is usually filled in one of two ways. A person may contribute part of each paycheque as it is earned, or move an existing lump sum, perhaps a non-registered holding, into the TFSA. Moving existing units in kind counts as a contribution at market value and can realize a gain in the non-registered account, as the in-kind contribution guide shows. Either way, the room is finite, so what goes into it matters.

Test missed strong months, missed weak months and a real exit window

That arrangement is authored, but it reflects an observation regulators make about real markets. FINRA notes that some of the top trading days occur during periods of greater volatility, so an investor who sells during a sharp but temporary decline may miss the rebound. The months that test nerves and the months that reward patience tend to arrive together.

The TFSA, not the fund, provides the tax shelter. Sheltering a bond fund avoids yearly tax on interest; sheltering an equity fund lets a higher but uncertain return compound without tax. Which helps more depends on the returns, the tax rates and the holding period, so test the placement rather than assume it.

The first chart shows CRA’s TFSA dollar limits. The limit was CAD 5,000 in 2009, CAD 10,000 in 2015, and has been CAD 7,000 for each of 2024, 2025 and 2026. That total applies only to someone who was 18 or older and resident in Canada since 2009 and has never contributed; your own room depends on your age, residency, contributions and withdrawals, and CRA’s My Account shows it.

The placements also differ in after-tax risk. The government shares part of the gains and, through loss offsets, part of the losses in a taxable account, but nothing in a TFSA. Two portfolios with the same pre-tax 40/60 mix can therefore carry different after-tax exposure. That is one reason to treat asset location as a refinement after the allocation is right, not a replacement for it.

The tax pattern differs much more than the result. Bond first pays about CAD 7,142 of tax on yearly income over the 20 years but leaves about CAD 17,855 of tax due on the final equity sale. Equity first pays about CAD 15,019 on yearly income, mostly interest, and only about CAD 5,952 on the sale. Deferral and the half inclusion rate make unrealized equity growth relatively tax-efficient outside the TFSA; interest has neither advantage.

The useful question is what happens to someone who follows a rule they could actually follow, such as “move to cash after this month-end and come back in six months.” This guide answers both with one authored ten-year path for an existing CAD 10,000 balance. The path is deliberately simple: calm months averaging about 0.5%, a 14-month crisis in months 41 to 54 in which large losses and large gains alternate, then a recovery. Any month spent out of the market earns cash interest, 2.25% a year by default.

This guide follows a balance already invested. Money arriving from each paycheque raises a different question: whether to keep investing it on schedule during a volatile period. Regular contributions keep buying through a window like the one above, including some of the low-priced months. Holding new pay in cash until conditions look better turns each deposit into a timing decision; the dip-waiting guide tests that rule, and the cash-floor guide checks whether contributions remain affordable if income stops.

Three placements are compared. Bond first puts all CAD 40,000 of bond fund in the TFSA and holds the equity fund outside. Equity first puts CAD 40,000 of equity fund in the TFSA and leaves the bond fund and the remaining equity outside. Same mix holds 40/60 in each account. Worry about a financial-crisis-style fall is reasonable, especially for money needed within a few years. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor education site suggests staying with a diversified portfolio that fits your plan and warns that trying to time the market can mean losses when prices drop and missed gains when they recover. Those points suggest acting on the allocation rather than the calendar:
Write a rebalancing rule in advance; the rebalancing guide shows how one behaves through a crash.
Year-end, assuming a sale of the non-registered holdings at that date
Years before the non-registered holdings are sold
bond interest is taxed every year at the entered marginal rate, 30% by default;
equity distributions are taxed every year at a separate entered rate, 15% by default, as a simple stand-in for a mix of dividends and capital gains distributions;
reinvested after-tax distributions raise the adjusted cost base, as CRA’s mutual-fund guidance describes;
unrealized price growth is taxed only when the units are sold, at the marginal rate times the one-half inclusion rate shown in CRA’s capital gains guidance.

“Missing the best days” and “avoiding the worst days” are hindsight exercises. In volatile stretches the best and worst periods sit side by side, so an exit usually skips some of each. Whether an exit helps depends on dates nobody knows in advance, which is why a written allocation usually serves crash worry better than a forecast.
